outOfScope: designing or evaluating a real program

claims.claim: For the specific organizational-sentencing purposes named in the guideline, U.S.S.G. §8B2.1 describes an effective compliance and ethics program as one reasonably designed, implemented, and enforced to prevent and detect criminal conduct and promote ethical conduct and legal compliance.

Section 8B2.1 lists standards and procedures, governing-authority oversight, assigned responsibility, practical communication and training, monitoring and auditing, a reporting or guidance system without fear of retaliation, consistent incentives and discipline, and appropriate response as program components for that guideline's purposes.
The guideline says organizations should periodically assess criminal-conduct risk and modify the listed requirements appropriately to reduce risks found through that process.

The Department of Justice's Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs is a framework prosecutors use when assessing corporate compliance programs in relevant DOJ matters; it asks whether a program is well designed, empowered to work in practice, and works in practice.

The DOJ framework discusses risk assessment, policies and procedures, training and communications, confidential reporting and investigation, incentives and discipline, continuous improvement, testing and review, and investigation of misconduct as assessment topics rather than a universal legal checklist for every organization.
Ethical standards and legal obligations overlap but are not identical; an action can be legal while still raising ethical concerns, and ethical views can differ among people and organizations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The word compliance can refer to legal duties, contractual requirements, licensing conditions, professional standards, internal commitments, or a federal enforcement and sentencing framework.
positions: U.S.S.G. §8B2.1 establishes terms for specified federal organizational sentencing provisions.
The DOJ ECCP guides prosecutors' assessment in relevant federal criminal matters.
Other organizations may be governed by different laws, regulators, contracts, locations, and risk profiles.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the federal sources as examples of widely taught program elements, identifies their limited institutional settings, and does not present them as a universal program design or a determination of any organization's obligations.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No prior compliance artifact existed for this planned topic.
correctionsNeeded: Created original, source-verified general-education coverage rather than a compliance template.
Qualified the sentencing guideline and DOJ framework by purpose and institution.
Separated legal obligations from ethical commitments without treating either as a substitute for the other.
Excluded real-program design, audit, reporting, and legal advice.
rightsIssues: All sources are used for reference only. The lesson is original explanatory prose and does not reproduce guideline or DOJ text beyond short names and concepts.
